name: Ben Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a dozer operator at an open-pit nickel mine, and I'm the lead hand for the dozer crew. Most days I'm pushing up material on the waste dumps, building ramps and cleaning up around the shovels so the trucks have a good floor to work on. For the last eight months I've also been part of a trial where one of our dozers is driven from a seat in a trailer, with cameras and a joystick. Honestly, the trailer's air conditioning is the best part, but the controls are good too.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into the trial?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I asked. I'm the kind of person who reads the manual for fun. I use AI every day, for my shift notes, for planning push patterns, even for checking my share portfolio on the weekend. When the company said they wanted someone senior to try the remote dozer, I said yes before my supervisor finished the sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, and that's fine. Plenty of good tools still came out of it. I'd probably post something like that on the mining forum I read, and say it at the crib table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't change my plans much. I'd keep working until sixty-two, maybe sixty-three, with good savings and some shares. I'd lose a bit on a couple of tech shares, but nothing that hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the job, keep using the AI tools I already use. I'd ask the company to keep the remote dozer trial going even if the big automation plans slowed down. And I'd probably rebalance my shares a little, out of the tech companies that overpromised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned shares. How much does that shape how you think about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite a lot, to be honest. I've got some money in a mining equipment company and a couple of tech names. I treat it like a hedge: if robots take mine jobs, at least I own a piece of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss in this quiet version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trailer, honestly. I've enjoyed learning something new at fifty-eight. I'd hate for them to scrap it and send me back to the bumpy seat for good.

S0.say: I'd say it was oversold, which is fine because plenty of good tools came out of it. I'd post that on the mining forum I read and say it at the crib table.
S0.think: Privately it doesn't change my plans to work until sixty-two or sixty-three with good savings and shares. I'd lose a bit on some tech shares, but nothing that hurts.
S0.do: Keeps working and using his AI tools, and asks the company to keep the remote dozer trial running. Moves some money out of tech shares that overpromised.
S0.quote: If robots take mine jobs, at least I own a piece of the robots.
S0.fieldNote: Ben is unusual in owning shares in mining equipment and tech companies as a deliberate hedge against automation. He genuinely enjoys learning and would miss the remote trial. He sees AI through the eyes of a small investor as much as a worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so get on board early. Learn the new systems before you're told to. I'd say it to the younger guys on the crew and I'd post about it on the forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. I'm already on the remote dozer, so I'd be one of the first people they'd want in the control room. I'd finish my career in air conditioning instead of on the dumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move to the remote operations team full-time in the first year, and I'd do whatever courses the company offered on supervising more than one machine at once. I'd put a bit more into the equipment company shares. And I'd help train the rest of the dozer crew, because if they're stuck, the whole crew gets cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would find it hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wiremu, who's been on dozers longer than me. He's brilliant on the machine but he hates screens. I'd sit with him on the remote seat and show him it's still pushing dirt, just with a different chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put more into shares. Is that a way of betting against your own crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about that. I don't think so, because the robots are coming whether I own the shares or not. I'd rather have a bit of the upside and use some of it to help my kids than pretend it's not happening.

S1.say: I'd say it's coming, so get on board early and learn new systems before you're told to. I'd tell the younger crew and post it on the forum.
S1.think: Privately it's good for me, since I'm already on the remote dozer and would be among the first wanted in the control room. I'd finish my career in air conditioning instead of on the dumps.
S1.do: Asks to join the remote operations team full-time in the first year and takes courses on supervising several machines. Puts more into equipment company shares and helps train the rest of the dozer crew.
S1.feel: Calm and actually a bit excited.
S1.quote: I'd finish my career in air conditioning instead of on the dumps.
S1.fieldNote: Ben sees Steady Disruption as an opportunity and is already positioned for it. He answered the question about betting against his crew honestly and without defensiveness. His plan to help Wiremu shows he cares about the crew as well as his own position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the real thing, and anyone who thinks it won't touch them should think again. I'd also say governments should have a plan ready, because two years is too fast for most people. I'd say that online and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I'm all right. I'd be sixty, I've got savings and shares, and I'd likely be in the control room until the end. My worry is my son Kofi. He's twenty-two and halfway through an electrical apprenticeship at the mine, and two years is right when he'd finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Kofi in the first week and look at where electricians would still be needed, probably in robot maintenance and the power side. I'd help him pay for extra courses in automation and controls. I'd move into the remote operations role straight away and stay as long as they'd have me. I'd also shift some savings into the equipment company, because that's where the work would be going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because of Kofi. For myself, I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years compare with the slower pictures for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, there's not much difference, I'd adapt in any of them. For Kofi it's huge. Two years means he finishes his ticket into a world that's already changed, with no time to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kofi that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the robots still need power, cables and someone to climb up and fix them in the rain. That's his trade. Then I'd tell him I'd pay for whatever course he picks, because that's what I've got the savings for.

S2.say: I'd say this is the real thing and anyone who thinks it won't touch them should think again, and governments need a plan ready. I'd say it online and at work.
S2.think: Privately I'm all right at sixty with savings, shares and a likely spot in the control room. My worry is my son Kofi, whose electrical apprenticeship finishes right when it hits.
S2.do: Sits down with Kofi in the first week to plan a move towards robot maintenance and offers to pay for automation courses. Moves straight into remote operations and shifts some savings into equipment company shares.
S2.feel: Uneasy because of his son, but fine for himself.
S2.quote: Two years means he finishes his ticket into a world that's already changed, with no time to steer.
S2.fieldNote: For Ben the time pressure matters through his son rather than himself. He would use his savings to fund Kofi's extra training, which is a concrete family plan. He is consistent across pictures: early adoption and investing in the companies building the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so use it. Get the training sorted now, at the companies and at the technical colleges. I'd post that on the forum and probably bore my wife Ama with it at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years works out well for me. I'd be sixty-three, about when I'd planned to stop. And Kofi would have three years after his ticket to move into robot maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the remote team in the first year, then try to get onto the commissioning crew when the fully automated dozers arrive, because I know the ground. I'd help Kofi plan his next step after the apprenticeship. And I'd look at doing some paid training for other sites after I retire, maybe a few weeks a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a plan I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes Kofi's story completely. With two years he's scrambling. With five, he can finish his ticket, get a year on the tools, then move across to automation with experience behind him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd do paid training after retiring. Would Ama be happy with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd want me out of the house, to be honest. She's a pharmacist and works part-time now. A few weeks a year somewhere warm, training operators, sounds like a good retirement to both of us.

S3.say: I'd say there's time, so use it to sort out training at companies and technical colleges. I'd post it on the forum and probably bore Ama with it at dinner.
S3.think: Privately five years works well, since I'd be sixty-three, around my planned stop. Kofi would have three years after his ticket to move into robot maintenance.
S3.do: Moves to the remote team in the first year and aims for the commissioning crew for automated dozers. Helps Kofi plan beyond his apprenticeship and plans paid training work at other sites after retiring.
S3.feel: Calm, with a plan he can work with.
S3.quote: A few weeks a year somewhere warm, training operators, sounds like a good retirement to both of us.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Ben exactly the shape he wants: a smooth handover into commissioning and a runway for his son. He thinks about retirement as an active phase with paid training work. He measures the time difference almost entirely through Kofi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so nobody should be caught out. Learn the tools, plan your next move, and don't wait for the company to tell you. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's very manageable. I'd be retired before it arrives. I'd probably own a few more robot company shares by then, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on the remote dozer and use the years to learn as much as I can about the automated systems, partly because I enjoy it. I'd keep adding to my investments slowly, the equipment company and a broad fund. Then I'd retire at sixty-two or sixty-three, as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like normal life with a new chapter at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Efua's studying law. Ten years is right when she'd be getting established, and the AI is already good at legal paperwork. I worry about her more than Kofi in this one, which surprised me just now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to be the lawyer who uses the AI best, not the one who pretends it isn't there. She'll roll her eyes, because she knows I'm the AI guy in the family. But she'll listen.

S4.say: I'd say a decade means nobody should be caught out, so learn the tools, plan your next move and don't wait for the company to tell you. I'd say it to anyone who asked.
S4.think: Privately it's very manageable, because I'd be retired before it arrives. I'd probably own a few more robot company shares by then, honestly.
S4.do: Keeps working on the remote dozer and learns as much as he can about automated systems. Keeps adding slowly to his investments and retires at 62 or 63 as planned.
S4.feel: Calm, like normal life with a new chapter at the end.
S4.quote: I worry about her more than Kofi in this one, which surprised me just now.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Ben's worry moved from his son to his daughter, who is studying law, and he noticed the shift himself. He remains steady and practical throughout. His advice to his daughter mirrors his own approach: be the person who uses the tools best.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of Kofi's timing, not mine. What would help is the technical college offering short courses in robot maintenance right now, so apprentices like him can add them on before they finish.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want to stay in the job if the robots took over. And I think I would, for a while. Somebody has to watch them, and I'd rather it was someone who's actually pushed dirt.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to watch them, and I'd rather it was someone who's actually pushed dirt.
portrait: Ben Mensah is a 58-year-old lead dozer operator at an open-pit nickel mine, already part of a trial running a dozer remotely from a trailer, and an everyday AI user. He has good savings and owns shares in mining equipment and tech companies as a deliberate hedge against automation. He is calm through most pictures and sees change as an opportunity to finish his career in the control room or commissioning crew. His only unease comes through his children: his son Kofi's apprenticeship timing in AGI by 2028, and his daughter Efua's law career in the ten-year picture. He is pragmatic, blames no one, and plans to use his savings to help his kids adjust.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his son Kofi would finish his electrical apprenticeship just as the change hit, with no time to steer.
whatWouldHelp: Short courses in robot maintenance at the technical college right now, so apprentices can add them before they finish.
